players.note: Tetairoa McMillan is the WR38 in fantasy points per game. He has an 18% target share, 1.60 YPRR, four red zone targets, five deep targets, and a 22.5% first-read share. The usage has been there for McMillan, but Young's volatile nature has had him riding a rollercoaster, with only 54.5% of his targets deemed catchable. This week, McMillan faces a Detroit secondary that has utilized the tenth-highest single-high rate (54.5%). This season, against single high, McMillan has seen more of the usage move in Jalen Coker's direction, as he has only a 17% target-per-route run rate and 1.00 YPRR against single high, but last year he had a 26% target-per-route run rate and 2.05 YPRR against single high. McMillan could see the usage move back in his direction this week with Coker limited or out.Â McMillan's range of outcomes is wide, but it could be fruitful this week. Detroit has allowed the sixth-most yards per target and the ninth-most fantasy points per opportunity to perimeter wide receivers.

Josh Downs is the WR33 in fantasy points per game, but he has produced much better than that fantasy ranking on a per-route basis. Downs has a 24.5% target share with 2.07 YPRR, four red zone targets, three deep targets, and a team-leading 31.5% first-read share. Downs has a stellar 0.133 first downs per route run. Downs should have another nice week against the Commanders, who since 2025 have allowed the second-most yards per target and the 12th-most fantasy points per opportunity to slot receivers. Downs will see a mild target bump with Keenan Allen out this week.Â

Well, apparently I prematurely forecasted Rashee Rice's demise after two lackluster weeks to open the season as the Chiefs' fourth target option. Last week, that changed massively. Rice led the team with a 37.5% target share, finishing with a 7.3 aDOT, 88 receiving yards (4.89 YPRR), two red zone targets, and a 38.9% first-read share (led the team by a WIDE margin). We'll see if Rice continues to see this alpha-type usage moving forward, but it was wonderful to witness if you roster Rice. This week, Rice will face a Raiders' secondary that has utilized two high with 57.5% (11th-highest rate) of their defensive snaps. Against two high, Rice leads the team with a 21% target per route run rate while posting a stellar 2.45 YPRR. Rice should see enough volume to overcome a surprisingly tough matchup this week. The Raiders have allowed the fewest yards per target and fantasy points per opportunity to perimeter wide receivers.

Matthew Golden is in the midst of a sophomore breakout season. Golden is the WR15 in fantasy points per game with a 22.6% target share, 2.32 YPRR, four red zone targets, six deep targets, and a 27.4% first-read share (leads the team). He has been absolutely awesome. I didn't know what to make of Golden this summer after a sleepy rookie season and minimal usage. This week, he'll face a Bucs secondary that has the second-highest single high rate in the NFL (71.7%). Against single high, he is second on the team with a 24% target-per-route run rate with only 1.43 YPRR. He has been the team's go-to against two high, with improved efficiency. This isn't a coffin nail, but it's harder to project a ceiling week for Golden when considering this. Tampa Bay hasn't been amazing at defending perimeter wide receivers, allowing the 13th-most yards per target and fantasy points per opportunity to the position. Golden can still have a strong Week 4, even if he doesn't blow the doors off.

Michael Wilson is the clear number two option in the Arizona passing attack as the WR21 in fantasy points per game. Wilson has a 25.6% target share with 1.38 YPRR, five red zone targets, three deep targets, and a 35.1% first-read share (leads the team). Wilson should have another productive outing in Week 4 against a secondary that has allowed the 11th-most fantasy points per opportunity to perimeter wide receivers, while ranking 18th in yards per target given up to the position.

Jaylen Waddle is the WR38 in fantasy points per game, as he has suffered through bad quarterback play and questionable play calling through three games. Over the last two games, Waddle has had a 26.2% target share, 3.08 YPRR, one red zone target, four deep targets, and a 35.1% first-read share. This week, he faces a 49ers secondary that has utilized single high at the eighth-highest rate (57.7%). Since Week 2, against single high, Waddle has had a 40% target-per-route-run rate and 3.32 YPRR. That's insane usage and production. If Nix can get his head on straight, Waddle should have a banner week. The 49ers have allowed the third-most yards per target and the fourth-most fantasy points per opportunity to slot receivers. Waddle was seen in a boot (foot) leaving last week's game, but he practiced in full to open this week.

DJ Moore has been an elite alpha in his two full games played with 16.8 PPR points per game. Overall, that would be the WR10 in fantasy points per game. In those two games, Moore has had ELITE usage and production with a 30.9% target share, 3.55 YPRR, two red zone targets, four deep targets, 0.170 FD/RR, and a 33.3% first-read share. Moore should be peppered with targets this week, and he gets a boost with no Christian Gonzalez (ruled out) to deal with this week. New England ranks 17th in fantasy points per opportunity allowed to perimeter wide receivers.

Last week, Jordan Addison operated as Minnesota's alpha with Justin Jefferson sidelined. Last week, in the final three quarters of the game, Addison had a 29.2% target share, an 80.3% air-yard share, and a 43.8% first-read share. In those three quarters, he finished with four grabs, four deep targets, and 86 receiving yards (3.19 YPRR). Overall, he finished with nine targets, five receptions, and 90 receiving yards (one score) as the WR13 for the week. Addison could easily be a top 15-20 wide receiver again this week. Over the last two games, Miami has had the ninth-highest two-high rate in the NFL (62%). Since 2023, against two-high, Addison has seen a bump in his target-per-route run rate from 18% to 20% and his YPRR from 1.50 to 1.83. I'm not scared of the Miami secondary that has allowed the 14th-most yards per target to perimeter wide receivers.

Stefon Diggs has had a strong start to his Washington tenure as the WR17 in fantasy points per game. Diggs is tied for the team lead with a 22% target share while producing 1.82 YPRR with four red zone targets (leads the team), three deep targets, and a 25.4% first-read share (second on the team). This week, Diggs faces an Indy pass defense that has utilized single high at the ninth-highest rate (57.1%). This season, against single high, Diggs has had a 30% target-per-route run rate and 2.19 YPRR. Diggs is a strong fantasy option this week against a pass defense that has allowed the most yards per target and the third-most fantasy points per opportunity to receivers. If Terry McLaurin misses Week 4, Diggs will operate as Washington's clear WR1. Diggs would be a WR2 with a volume-based WR3 floor.

Last week, Malik Nabers was back to a full workload with an 81% snap rate, a 76.9% route share, a 27.3% target share, only 26 receiving yards (1.30 YPRR), and a 37.5% first-read share (one red zone target). The result wasn't amazing, but it's great to see Nabers back to a full-time role. Now, he just needs better quarterback play on the field to turn this type of market share into on-field production. Nabers should at least see enough catchable targets this week to take advantage of a nice matchup. The Cards have allowed the most yards per target and the third-most fantasy points per opportunity to perimeter wide receivers.

Well, we finally got to see the Luther Burden that was promised last week. He finished as the WR13 for the week. It looks like Ben Johnson bought all of his summer stock for Burden back. Burden has a 23.5% target share with 1.95 YPRR, six red zone targets (leads the team), zero deep targets, and a 32.8% first-read share (leads the team). This week, he faces a Jets' secondary that has the fifth-highest two-high rate in the NFL (65.4%). Against two high, Burden is second on the team with a 21% target-per-route run rate with only 0.79 YPRR. Last week, against two high, he had a 36% target per route run rate (led the team). I'm not worried about the small-sample inefficiency against two high, as he had 1.88 YPRR against two high last year with a 25% target-per-route run rate. Burden should have another busy game in Week 4 against a secondary that has ranked 15th in yards per target against slot receivers.

The Chargers' passing attack is a confounding mess. It's difficult to feel good about playing anyone on that roster right now. Ladd McConkey came out of the gate hot in Week 1 until he snapped a rib, and he has been middling ever since. Last week, McConkey had a 14.7% target share (third on the team) with a 19% first-read share (third on the team). He was a full-time player, though, with an 87.5% snap rate and 84.2% route share. It's maddening. It feels like Mike McDaniel is scrambling in real time to make this all work and flailing while doing so. McConkey is second on the team in red zone targets (two) and deep targets (two). McConkey could lead the team in targets this week, or he could be the third option in the passing progressions. Who knows. I do know that I don't want to plug him into a lineup this week against a secondary that has allowed the fourth-fewest yards per target and the tenth-fewest fantasy points per opportunity to perimeter wide receivers. McConkey picked up a new foot injury last week to add on top of his tender ribs. McConkey was limited in practice on Wednesday and Friday. He missed practice on Thursday. That's not an encouraging set of practice reports. He has been listed as questionable for Week 4.

Devaughn Vele was due for a down week, and it happened last week, but he is still the WR23 in fantasy points per game. Vele has a 16.7% target share with 1.32 YPRR, three red zone targets, four deep targets, and a 20.4% first-read share. Vele faces an Atlanta secondary that has utilized single high at the fifth-highest rate (64.7%). Against single high, Vele has an 18% target-per-route run rate and a strong 1.91 YPRR. Vele is a solid flex play with a tough matchup. Atlanta has held slot receivers to the fifth-fewest yards per target and the second-fewest fantasy points per opportunity this season.

After a down Week 3, Dontayvion Wicks has slipped to WR32 in fantasy points per game. Wicks has a 17% target share, 2.29 YPRR, four red zone targets, four deep targets, and a 23.2% first-read share. After a dip last week, Wicks saw his route share bounce back to 77.4% last week. We'll see if Wicks can bounce back this week after a disappointing stat line against the Bears, but he'll be operating as the top target in the Philly passing attack this week. With DeVonta Smith and Dallas Goedert out and Makal Lemon still finding his NFL footing, Wicks should be the receiver Hurts leans on in Week 4. This week, he'll tangle with a Rams pass defense that has featured two high with 58.3-60% of their defensive snaps in two of their three games. Against two high, Wicks has a 21% target-per-route run rate and 2.91 YPRR. Wicks is a solid flex play again this week with WR2 upside. The Rams have held perimeter receivers to the 14th-fewest yards per target, but they have also allowed the 12th-most fantasy points per opportunity to the position.

Oh, the yearly struggle with rostering Jameson Williams. He's the WR57 in fantasy points per game this season, and it has been a bumpy ride. Williams has a 10% target share, 1.19 YPRR, zero red zone targets, one deep target, and a 14% first-read share. I don't know if Williams' struggles are resolved this week. Carolina has the fifth-highest single high rate in the NFL (63.5%). Williams has been an afterthought against single high this season with an 11% target-per-route run rate and 0.70 YPRR. It's possible that he does bounce back this week, though. Last year, Williams had a 22% target-per-route run rate and 2.31 YPRR against single high. Carolina has been tough against perimeter wide receivers, but they just lost Jaycee Horn, so take these numbers with a grain of salt. Carolina has allowed the sixth-fewest yards per target and fourth-fewest fantasy points per opportunity to perimeter wide receivers. Williams is a volatile flex play this week, but his ceiling is sky-high if his usage changes against a matchup that isn't as scary as it seems on paper.

Jakobi Meyers is the WR30 in fantasy points per game with two top-30 finishes in weekly scoring through three games (WR28, WR14). Meyers has a 13.6% target share, 1.89 YPRR, two red zone targets (two scores), one deep target, and a 17.2% first-read share. I expect DJ Turner to follow Brian Thomas Jr. this week, but after seeing Thomas Jr.'s role in the offense decline last week, I could be wrong. Meyers could see Turner this week, so there's volatility in his projection. Turner has shadowed in each game this season following Emeka Egbuka, Xavier Hutchinson, and DK Metcalf on 53.1-69% of their routes. Turner hasn't allowed any of these receivers to surpass 53 receiving yards in his coverage. Metcalf scored a touchdown against him, but Turner ran into a teammate on the play, which left Metcalf wide open. Meyers is downgraded this week with a possible shadow and the fact that Cincy has been tough against perimeter wide receivers, allowing the second-fewest yards per target and the fourth-fewest fantasy points per opportunity to the position.

Deebo Samuel is the WR22 in fantasy points per game, seeing a 13.3% target share with 2.84 YPRR, three red zone targets, zero deep targets, and a 14% first-read share. He has been the clear fourth option in the passing attack for San Francisco. Denver has mostly held receivers in check this season, but with Samuel's multifaceted role (four rushing attempts, 30 rushing yards) and Brock Purdy playing out of his mind, he's a flex option this week. Denver has allowed the 14th-most yards per target to wide receivers while holding them to the tenth-fewest fantasy points per opportunity.

DK Metcalf has started the season slowly as the WR47 in fantasy points per game. Metcalf has a 20.9% target share with only 0.82 YPRR, seven deep targets, one red zone target, and a 31.4% first-read share. He has seen solid volume weekly and done very little with it. Last week, he scored a touchdown as DJ Turner ran into a teammate, thus leaving Metcalf wide open in the end zone. This week, he faces a Cleveland pass defense that has the highest single-high rate (75.7%) in the NFL. Against single high, Metcalf has struggled this season with only a 19% target per route run rate and 0.61 YPRR. I expect another disappointing stat line from Metcalf this week. After their Week 1 debacle, the Browns' secondary has tightened up, allowing the seventh-fewest yards per target and the fifth-fewest fantasy points per opportunity to perimeter wide receivers over the last two weeks.

Malik Washington has been a volume-filled low-end flex play this season as the WR48 in fantasy points per game. Washington has a 26.7% target share, 1.65 YPRR, one red zone target, six deep targets, and a 26.7% first-read share. Despite this high-volume usage, Washington hasn't eclipsed 12 PPR points in any game this season. This isn't the week to decide to flex him. Minnesota has allowed the ninth-fewest yards per target and fantasy points per opportunity to slot receivers.

With Cam Ward struggling to provide even league-average quarterback play, Carnell Tate has been the WR49 in fantasy points per game. Tate has a team-leading 22.7% target share with 1.46 YPRR, one red zone target, one deep target, and a 31% first-read share. Until Ward shows some promise, Tate will continue to struggle to post nice stat lines. Baltimore isn't the place to look to plug him into a fantasy lineup. The Ravens have limited perimeter wide receivers to the tenth-fewest yards per target and eighth-fewest fantasy points per opportunity.

Emeka Egbuka is the WR33 in fantasy points per game, but the lack of production isn't his fault necessarily. Only 65% of his targets have been catchable. Among 86 qualifying receivers, Egbuka ranks 19th in separation and 15th in route win rate, so he's doing exactly what he's supposed to be doing. Getting open early and often. Egbuka has a 20.2% target share with 1.48 YPRR, two red zone targets, three deep targets, and a 24.6% first-read share. This week, he faces a Green Bay pass defense that has the sixth-highest two-high rate (64.4%). Against two high, Egbuka has led the team with a 21% target-per-route run rate and 1.92 YPRR. If rookie Jalon Daniels can get him the ball, Egbuka could surprise people this week against a secondary that has allowed the 12th-most yards per target and the sixth-most fantasy points per opportunity to perimeter wide receivers.

Denzel Boston finally wasn't able to overcome his struggling quarterback last week, producing only 8.1 PPR points. Overall, he is the WR19 in fantasy points per game. Boston has an 18.1% target share, 2.27 YPRR, three red zone targets, four deep targets, and a 21.4% first-read share (second on the team). Boston could overcome Deshaun Watson's struggles again this week if he sees catchable targets. The Steelers have allowed the fourth-most yards per target and the fifth-most fantasy points per opportunity to perimeter wide receivers.

Last week, Wan'Dale Robinson had easily his best showing of the season as the WR18 for the week. Robinson's issues have also been tied to Cam Ward. Robinson has a 20.5% target share with 1.33 YPRR, three red zone targets, one deep target, and a 27.6% first-read share (second on the team). Robinson could be a decent PPR or volume-based flex this week. Baltimore has allowed the ninth-most yards per target and the 12th-most fantasy points per opportunity to slot receivers.

Over the last two games, Doubs has been the WR23 and WR54 in weekly scoring with a 15.1% target share, 3.22 YPRR, one red zone target, one deep target, and a 14.7% first-read share. This hasn't been the usage anyone was hoping for with AJ Brown out of the lineup. We could see Doubs bounce back this week, though. It's possible that he sees shadow coverage from Christian Benford (if he plays) but I doubt that Buffalo is concerned enough with Doubs to put Benford on him. Doubs could be the go-to for Drake Maye this week against Buffalo's two-high coverage. Buffalo has the tenth-highest two-high rate (58.1%). Since Week 2, against two-high, Doubs has been the leader in target-per-route run rate with 22% and 6.13 YPRR(!!). Since 2025, Doubs has seen a boost against two high with a 21% target-per-route run rate and 2.16 YPRR. If Benford doesn't follow Doubs, he should have a strong game this week. Buffalo is 15th in yards per target and fantasy points per opportunity allowed to perimeter wide receivers.

KC Concepcion is the WR69 in fantasy points per game, despite leading the Browns with a 22.9% target share. Sadly, with their struggling quarterback, Concepcion has only 1.01 YPRR, two red zone targets, and a deep target while leading the team with a 30.4% first-read share. Concepcion is likely a low-end flex play again this week against a Pittsburgh secondary that ranks 16th in yards per target allowed to slot receivers while also giving up the eighth-fewest fantasy points per opportunity to the position.

Courtland Sutton has started VERY slowly as Bo Nix struggles to support anyone in this passing attack week-to-week. Sutton is the WR80 in fantasy points per game with only a 16.1% target share, 1.04 YPRR, five red zone targets, two deep targets, and a 21.6% first-read share. This week, he faces a 49ers secondary that has utilized single high at the eighth-highest rate (57.7%). Since Week 2, against single high, Sutton has had only an 18% target per route run rate and 1.57 YPRR. Last year, he crushed single high with a 26% target per route run rate and 2.32 YPRR. It's asking a lot of Nix to support multiple pass catchers at the moment, but if Nix can snap out of his funk, Sutton does have some flex value in a tough matchup. The 49ers have allowed the sixth-fewest yards per target and the seventh-fewest fantasy points per opportunity to perimeter wide receivers.

After three games, Kalif Raymond is the WR14 in fantasy points per game. His usage looks real, and we should all stand up and take notice. Raymond has a 20.4% target share with 2.85 YPRR, three red zone targets, one deep target, and a 23% first-read share (second on the team). We'll see if he keeps this up, but he looks legit. This week, he faces a Jets' secondary that has the fifth-highest two-high rate in the NFL (65.4%). Against two-high, Raymond leads the team with a 22% target-per-route run rate with 2.00 YPRR. Raymond is a solid flex with a tougher matchup. New York has allowed the seventh-fewest yards per target to perimeter wide receivers while ranking 17th in fantasy points per opportunity allowed.

Rome Odunze has been the forgotten man in Chicago's passing attack as the WR58 in fantasy points per game. Odunze has only a 13.3% target share with 1.72 YPRR, two red zone targets, five deep targets, and a 13.1% first-read share. This week, he faces a Jets' secondary that has the fifth-highest two-high rate in the NFL (65.4%). Against two-high, Odunze's target-per-route run rate drops from 18% to 14%, and his yards per route run dips from 2.00 to 1.38. Odunze is only a middling flex play this week against a secondary that has allowed the seventh-fewest yards per target to perimeter wide receivers while ranking 17th in fantasy points per opportunity allowed.

Over the last two games, Mack Hollins has led the Patriots with a 20.8% target share with 2.39 YPRR, three red zone targets, a deep target, and a 26.5% first-read share. These are strong usage and production metrics across the board. Hollins is a solid flex play this week, although I don't know if he'll retain his top spot in the passing attack in Week 4. Buffalo has the tenth-highest two-high rate (58.1%). Since Week 2, against two-high, Hollins has been second on the team with a 17% target-per-route run rate with a stellar 2.46 YPRR. Since 2025, against two-high, Hollins has had a 19% target-per-route run rate and 2.05 YPRR against two-high. Buffalo is 15th in yards per target and fantasy points per opportunity allowed to perimeter wide receivers.

The Bills' passing attack has flowed through DJ Moore and Dalton Kincaid this season, which has left Khalil Shakir on the outside looking in. Shakir is the WR75 in fantasy points per game. He has a 16.4% target share, 1.37 YPRR, four red zone targets, zero deep targets, and an 18.5% first-read share. Shakir is a sit this week. New England has allowed the seventh-fewest yards per target to slot receivers. Yes, they have given up two receiving scores to slot receivers, but they both came last week, with Parker Washington and Josh Cameron getting into the end zone.

This is what Tre Tucker does. He pops off with the occasional big game, and then fantasy gamers are left chasing that high. Last week, Tucker came back to earth. In Weeks 1 and 3, Tucker has had only a 12.7% target share, 1.30 YPRR, one red zone target, zero deep targets, and a 15% first-read share. None of these metrics are anything to write home about. This week, he faces a Kansas City secondary that has held perimeter wide receivers to the third-fewest yards per target and fantasy points per opportunity. Tucker is an easy sit.

Xavier Worthy's role cratered last week. After fighting for second or third in the target pecking order over the previous games, Worthy fell to the bottom of the pile with an 8.3% target share, 1.06 YPRR, zero red-zone and deep targets, and a 5.6% first-read share (last among the Chiefs starters). Worthy is an easy sit this week. The Raiders have allowed the fewest yards per target and fantasy points per opportunity to perimeter wide receivers.

With Philly losing pass catchers to injuries, Makai Lemon will be thrust into a larger role this week. Overall, he has an 80.2% route share (83.9% last week), a 10.2% target share, 0.45 YPRR, zero red zone targets, one deep target, and a 12.5% first-read share. The Eagles are still trying to figure out how to best deploy him. He had a negative aDOT and a 50% designed target rate in Week 1. Over the last two weeks, Lemon has seen aDOTs of 14.0 and 11.7 with slot rates of 48.4% and 73.1%. Lemon is a deeper league flex this week because he will see decent volume, although I'm worried about his production and efficiency to this point. Among 86 qualifying receivers, Lemon ranks 42nd in separation and 73rd in route win rate. The matchup, at least, is interesting, with the Rams allowing the 12th-fewest yards per target to slot receivers while giving up the sixth-most fantasy points per opportunity to the position.

There's no way I'm playing Quentin Johnston in any league this week. Johnston has only a 17% target share with 0.79 YPRR and a 22% first-read share. Johnston leads the team with three deep targets, but he has zero red zone targets. Seattle has allowed the fourth-fewest yards per target and the tenth-fewest fantasy points per opportunity to perimeter wide receivers.

Despite posting a struggle bus stat line last week, Michael Pittman Jr. had a 70.3% route share, so he was close to a full-time player for the Steelers on passing plays. Pittman has had a sleepy start to his Steelers career with a 10.7% target share, 1.19 YPRR, zero deep or red zone targets, and a 9.1% first-read share. This week, he faces a Cleveland pass defense that has the highest single-high rate (75.7%) in the NFL. Against single-high, Pittman has had only a 9% target-per-route-run rate and 1.14 YPRR. Sit Pittman again this week. After their Week 1 debacle, the Browns' secondary has tightened up, allowing the seventh-fewest yards per target and the fifth-fewest fantasy points per opportunity to perimeter wide receivers over the last two weeks.

Rashod Bateman returned to the shadow realm last week with Zay Flowers active. In the two games this season that Flowers has played, Bateman has had an 8.9% target share with 0.80 YPRR, one red zone target, zero deep targets, and a 12.1% first-read share. Bateman is essentially Flowers' handcuff. He's a must-sit with Flowers back in the lineup.

Brian Thomas Jr. has had a predictable but rough beginning to the season. Last week, his route share dipped to 43.8% while he had only a 3.4% target share. Thomas Jr. is an easy sit this week with his role declining in the Jags offense and possible shadow coverage from DJ Turner when he's on the field. I don't know if Cincy will view Jakobi Meyers as the bigger threat this week or Thomas Jr., but Cincy has also been tough against perimeter receivers. Thomas Jr. is a sit, regardless of how you dice up this matchup. Turner has shadowed in each game this season following Emeka Egbuka, Xavier Hutchinson, and DK Metcalf on 53.1-69% of their routes. Turner hasn't allowed any of these receivers to surpass 53 receiving yards in his coverage. Metcalf scored a touchdown against him, but Turner ran into a teammate on the play, which left Metcalf wide open. Cincy has allowed the second-fewest yards per target and the fourth-fewest fantasy points per opportunity to perimeter wide receivers.

Chris Godwin has looked cooked through three games as the WR59 in fantasy points per game. Godwin has an 11.1% target share with 1.14 YPRR, zero red zone targets, zero deep targets, and a 14.5% first-read share. Among 86 qualifying receivers, he ranks 57th in separation and 49th in route win rate. This week, he faces a Green Bay pass defense that has the sixth-highest two-high rate (64.4%). Against two-high, Godwin has only an 8% target-per-route run rate and 0.33 YPRR. Sit Godwin this week. Green Bay has allowed the tenth-fewest yards per target to slot receivers while ranking 17th in fantasy points per opportunity allowed.

At this point, the Cards should trade Marvin Harrison Jr. He isn't part of the offensive game plan weekly, with only a 6.8% target share (18.6 aDOT) and 9.1% first-read share. Harrison Jr. is just running clear-out routes for the rest of the pass catchers on the depth chart. He's droppable.

Mike Evans sustained a rib injury last week. He opened this week with DNPs on Wednesday and Thursday. He managed a limited practice session on Friday. It sounds like Mike Evans is going to attempt to play through this rib issue this week. If he is active, I don't expect him to be a full-time player this week, but we'll see what news comes out on Saturday. I'll update his outlook on Saturday. Evans has been highly involved this season when on the field with a 30% target per route run rate, 2.58 YPRR, and a 22.8% first-read share. Evans has two red zone targets. If he is active and limited, I would expect him to be heavily involved in the red zone. Denver isn't a pushover against perimeter wide receivers, allowing the 11th-fewest fantasy points per opportunity to the position.

Last week, Miami continued to ramp up Chris Bell's usage as he had a 64.3% route share, a 19.4% target share, 67 receiving yards (2.48 YPRR, and a 16.7% first-read share. Bell had one deep target and zero red zone targets. We'll see if his role continues to grow this week, but he's an interesting flex play. Minnesota has allowed the 11th-most yards per target and the tenth-most fantasy points per opportunity to perimeter wide receivers. Bell (knee) had limited practice sessions on Wednesday and Thursday before upgrading to a full practice on Friday. I won't be shocked if he contends with Malik Washington for the team lead in targets this week.

Jalen Coker sustained a quad injury last week. Coker didn't practice on Wednesday, but he has limited sessions on Thursday and Friday. He has been listed as questionable. Dave Canales stated that the team would reevaluate Coker on Saturday to see if he can suit up this week. They elevated Ja'Seem Reed, which is a move that Canales said the team would make if Coker was out. I'm approaching this week as if he'll be sidelined. If Coker were to somehow play, I don't think he'll be a full-time option in Week 4. Coker has a 26% target-per-route run rate, 2.61 YPRR, and a 23.9% first-read share this season. When he would be on the field, I'd expect him to be heavily involved. He's facing a defense that has allowed the seventh-most yards per target and the ninth-most fantasy points per opportunity to perimeter wide receivers. Coker could get it done as a flex in Week 4, but lower your expectations some, as his route share will probably get cut somewhat.
